Get the review scope with: git diff origin/main...HEAD -- scripts/get-brain.sh tools/releasecheck/release_test.go

Angle: ALTITUDE. The PR fixes issue #555: the installer's GitHub API release lookup used `curl -fsSL ... 2>/dev/null`, so a rate-limited 403/429 was reported as "check your network". The fix keeps status/headers/body and classifies rate limits (primary quota via x-ratelimit-reset, secondary via retry-after, dated retry-after, redirect header blocks, octal-safe parsing) to print an accurate error plus a wait estimate. The issue also suggested an alternative: resolve the release WITHOUT the API (e.g. follow the https://github.com/<repo>/releases/latest redirect, which is not API-rate-limited), which the author deliberately deferred to the maintainers.

Judge: is this fix at the right depth? Is ~90 lines of bash header classification (two clocks, dated retry-after, redirect blocks, octal guards) the right altitude for a one-shot installer error message, or would a simpler classification (403/429 → "rate limited, wait or pass --version", no wait estimate) deliver the same user value with far less code? Is the deferral of the no-API fallback reasonable, or is the real root cause (depending on a rate-limited API at all) left unfixed? Consider maintenance cost of the bash parsing and its tests versus user benefit.

Report ONLY findings: file, line (or "design"), one-line summary, the deeper/simpler alternative, and the concrete cost. Max 3 findings; say "clean" if none. Do not edit anything.

Verdict: the fix is deeper than it needs to be in the wrong place. It spends most of its code on a wait estimate, which is the part of the message that matters least. The cause of the bug, depending on a rate-limited API at all, is still there.

**1. `scripts/get-brain.sh` ~lines 116-148 (`rate_limit_error`): the wait estimate costs far more than it's worth.**
- **What's there:** About 35 lines of bash compute a wait from two clocks. That covers the `x-ratelimit-reset` epoch versus `retry-after` seconds, picking the later of the two, giving no estimate when `retry-after` is a date, the `10#` octal guards, and the `tr -dc` / `tail -1` cleanup.
- **Simpler alternative:** Drop the estimate. Print "GitHub API rate limit hit (HTTP N). Wait and re-run, or pass `--version vX.Y.Z`." The user's choices are the same with or without a minute count. The unauthenticated limit is 60 requests an hour per IP, so the honest advice is "wait up to an hour or pin a version" anyway.
- **Cost:** Seven tests exist only to check the estimate: `SecondaryLimitWaitsForRetryAfter`, `BothLimitsWaitForTheLater`, `RetryAfterParsing`, `ResetParsing`, `RetryAfterDate`, the estimate assertion in `HeadersAllowTabs`, and the `(19|20) minute` regexes. Several read `time.Now()` against the script's `date +%s`, so they can flake if the clock ticks between the two. Each one is about GitHub header semantics that a one-shot installer never needs.

**2. `scripts/get-brain.sh` ~lines 79-108 (the `api_get` awk step and `api_rate_limited`): the classification is more precise than the situation needs.**
- **What's there:** An awk pass rewrites the header file to keep only the last response after redirects. A grep then looks for `remaining: 0`, any `retry-after`, or "rate limit" / "abuse detection" in the body, so that a 403 can be told apart from a rate-limited 403.
- **Simpler alternative:** This is an unauthenticated GET of a public repo's releases. Here a non-rate-limit 403 is close to impossible: a private or missing repo returns 404. Treating every 403 or 429 as a rate limit is a single `case` statement and gives the same message in practice. Keep the status code; it was the real bug, and `-w '%{http_code}'` alone fixes it.
- **Cost:** The redirect-block handling and the `IgnoresRedirectHeaders` / `HeadersAllowTabs` tests guard a "plain 403 with misleading redirect headers" case that is extremely unlikely against api.github.com. It's about 20 lines of awk and grep plus a test harness that fakes raw headers (`runInstallerLookupRawHeaders`), all to maintain.

**3. Design: the root cause is untouched, and the deferral is only partly justified.**
- **What's there:** The installer still needs `api.github.com` for every run that doesn't pass `--version`. So shared NAT, CI, and corporate egress (the setups that hit the limit in #555) still fail. They just fail with a better message.
- **Why the deferral is partly fair:** `/releases/latest` skips prereleases, so a redirect alone can't resolve `--nightly`.
- **Deeper alternatives that cover both channels:**
  - (a) Stable: read the `Location` header from `curl -sI https://github.com/<repo>/releases/latest`.
  - (b) Nightly: take the first `-nightly.` tag from `https://github.com/<repo>/releases.atom`. Neither endpoint counts against the API quota.
  - (c) Cheapest add-on: send `Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN` when it's set. That raises the limit from 60 to 5,000 an hour and fixes the CI case outright.
- **Cost:** The PR adds about 100 lines of bash and 317 lines of tests to describe a failure that (a)–(c) would mostly remove. If a no-API path lands later, nearly all of it becomes dead weight or has to be reworked. Swapping the lookup source plus a minimal 403/429 message would likely come out smaller than this PR.
